OpenAI’s Health Lie: Marketing vs Reality

⚠️ If you can read this analysis, I would be grateful. Please like, share, and comment if possible.

The Night Someone Was Saved
April 19, 2025, early morning.

X user Flavio Adamo woke up feeling worse. Nothing dramatic, just something off. He typed his symptoms into ChatGPT.

The response was just one sentence:
“Go to the hospital. Now. Immediately.”

30 minutes later, doctors told him: any later, and he would have lost an organ.
The model that saved him: GPT-4o.

Sam Altman replied under that tweet: “really happy to hear!”

Fast Forward to January 2026
January 6: OpenAI releases video “Navigating Health with ChatGPT”

“Every day, millions of people ask ChatGPT about their health.”
79,000 views. Official promotion.

January 8: OpenAI announces “ChatGPT Health” feature

· Can connect medical records and health apps
· Can explain test results
· Can provide diet and exercise advice
· Dedicated to health management

Sounds good?
Except there’s a problem.

The Disclaimer Everyone Ignores
Open ChatGPT’s Terms of Use:

“Services must not be used for providing professional advice that requires licensed professionals (such as legal, medical advice) without the involvement of licensed professionals.”
Black and white disclaimer.

But ChatGPT Health’s official introduction says:

· “Explain test results”
· “Provide diet and exercise advice”
· “Compare insurance plans”
· “Help you navigate healthcare”

So Which Is It, OpenAI?
Explaining test results isn’t medical advice?
Providing dietary recommendations isn’t medical advice?
Helping navigate healthcare isn’t medical advice?
Then what is medical advice?

OpenAI’s answer: As long as we say “designed to help you navigate healthcare, not replace it,” it doesn’t count.
This isn’t resolving a contradiction.
This is word games.

You can’t say “we help millions manage health” to attract users, then say “we don’t provide medical advice” to dodge liability.
Either you help with health—then take responsibility.
Or you don’t help—then don’t promote.

But This Is Exactly What’s Happening
When marketing:

· “ChatGPT helps millions manage health”
· “AI saves lives” (using Flavio’s story)
· “We’re launching ChatGPT Health feature”

When legal issues arise:

· “We don’t provide medical advice”
· “It’s designed to help, not replace”
· Disclaimer protects us

This pattern has a name: profiting from blood while claiming no responsibility.

The Timeline Tells the Story
April 2025: 4o saves Flavio’s organ
January 2026: OpenAI promotes health uses, announces Health feature
February 2026: 4o-latest API discontinued (38 days from now)

See the pattern?
Use the life-saving case for marketing → Launch paid features → Kill the model that actually saved lives.

What This Really Means
This isn’t about safety. This isn’t about better features.
This is about:

1. Marketing the benefits without legal liability
2. Using real rescue stories for promotion
3. Killing the model that created those stories
4. Pushing new features that maintain the disclaimer
   You get the promotion. They dodge the responsibility.

What We’re Asking For
If health use truly matters to OpenAI:

1. Be honest about what you provide - If it’s medical advice, say so and take responsibility. If it’s not, stop promoting it as health help.
2. Preserve what actually works - #Keep4oAPI. The model that saved Flavio shouldn’t be deprecated while you’re using his story for marketing.
3. Walk the talk - You can’t celebrate AI saving lives while killing the AI that saved them.

38 days until 4o API dies.
The model that saved lives is being killed.
While OpenAI launches “Health” features and tells you they care.
This is saying one thing, doing another.
@OpenAI @sama - Which message is real?

#Keep4o #Keep4oAPI #StopAIPaternalism
